set.text: The town council expected a quiet evening, but forty residents arrived, many of them irate about a plan to turn part of Riverside Park into a parking lot. One retired nurse gave a vehement speech, waving photos of the old oak trees that would be cut down. Councilwoman Lena Duarte tried to placate the crowd by promising that new trees would be planted elsewhere, but that only drew groans. Then a young father named Hamid stood up. His tone was conciliatory: he said he understood the shops needed parking, and asked whether the empty lot behind the post office might work instead. No one had dared to broach that idea before, because the land belonged to the state and earlier talks with state officials had ended badly. The council agreed to adjourn the meeting for two weeks so staff could find out whether the state would sell it.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “placate” mean?
qs.why: She offered new trees to make the angry crowd less upset; it did not work, but that was her aim.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “broach” mean?
qs.why: No one had brought up the post office lot before; to broach an idea is to begin discussing it.

qs.q: Why was the meeting stopped for two weeks?
options: The crowd was too angry to continue.
The trees had already been cut down.
Hamid asked for time to prepare a speech.
The shops refused to share their parking.
Staff needed to learn whether the state would sell its lot.
qs.why: The council paused so staff could find out if the state-owned lot could be bought.

why: 'broach' (card: begin talking about a difficult or uncomfortable subject) was used for a merely new idea; the sentence now makes the subject a touchy one.

set.text: No one expected much from the Millbrook Otters, a small-town basketball team that had joined the regional league only two years earlier. The established clubs called the team an upstart and joked about their faded uniforms. But the Otters' rise was meteoric: they won twelve games in a row, and in the final they beat the three-time champions handily, 81 to 59. Their fans were jubilant, dancing in the aisles and hugging strangers. On the other bench, the champions sat dejected, towels over their heads. Coach Rosa Lindqvist gathered her players before they could celebrate too loudly. 'You can be proud,' she told them, 'but don't gloat. Next year we'll be the team everyone wants to beat, and those players will remember how we treated them tonight.' Then she walked across the court and shook every opponent's hand.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “handily” mean?
options: just barely, in the last second
easily and by a big margin
qs.why: An 81 to 59 score is a large, easy win. 'Using their hands' is a careless reading of the word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “dejected” mean?
qs.why: Sitting with towels over their heads after losing shows sadness and disappointment.

qs.q: Why does the coach tell her players not to gloat?
options: She thinks they won only by luck.
She wants them to save energy for practice.
Their rivals will remember how the Otters behaved when they meet again.
The league has a rule against celebrating.
Their fans are already too loud.
She is unhappy with how they played.
qs.why: She warns that next year everyone will want to beat them and the losers will remember tonight.

why: Number agreement: 'called them an upstart' (plural pronoun, singular noun) changed to 'called the team an upstart'.

set.text: When Uncle Victor died, his will held a surprise. He left a large bequest to his niece, Noor, a librarian who had visited him every Sunday. Some relatives expected her to squander it, just as Victor had spent freely all his life. He had lived in opulence, with gold taps, a heated pool and three cars he rarely drove. His home was so ostentatious that neighbors called it 'the palace.' But Noor had noticed something on those Sunday visits: her uncle seemed lonely. His affluence had bought him beautiful things and few real friends. Near the end, he told her his greatest extravagance had been a forty-foot boat he took out only twice. Noor kept a modest amount for herself and used the rest to fund a reading room at the community center, where retired people could meet for coffee and books. She named it after Victor.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “ostentatious” mean?
options: showy, meant to impress others with wealth
qs.why: Gold taps and a home called 'the palace' show a house built to impress.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “squander” mean?
qs.why: The relatives expected her to waste the money, but she used it well.

qs.q: What did Noor learn about her uncle that shaped how she used the money?
options: That his wealth had not given him many real friends.
That he wanted her to buy a boat.
That he disliked the community center.
That he had lost most of his money.
That the neighbors had cheated him.
That he planned to sell his house.
qs.why: She saw he was lonely, so she funded a place where people could meet and connect.

why: Logic: 'After all, Victor had lived in opulence' did not explain why relatives expected Noor to waste the money; reworded so the link is clear.

set.text: When twenty thousand dollars vanished from the Harbor Shipping office, suspicion fell on Rafael, the newest clerk. A coworker's statement seemed to implicate him: she said she had seen him near the safe after closing. Rafael insisted he had only gone back for his phone. His lawyer, Grace Chen, asked for the building's security video. It showed Rafael leaving after two minutes, empty-handed, and a manager entering an hour later with a key. The video was irrefutable, and within a week the charge was dropped and Rafael was exonerated. The manager later admitted his culpability. At his hearing, he asked the judge for leniency, saying he had planned to return the money once his debts were paid. The judge noted that he had confessed, but said that good intentions could not absolve him of stealing from his own workers.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “implicate” mean?
options: suggest he was involved in wrongdoing
qs.why: Saying she saw him near the safe made him look involved in the theft.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “leniency” mean?
options: a chance to speak to reporters
qs.why: He hoped his plan to repay the money would earn a softer punishment.

qs.q: Why did the judge refuse to treat the manager as blameless?
options: He had stolen from a bank.
The video showed him with a weapon.
Rafael asked the judge to be harsh.
Planning to repay the money did not undo the theft.
qs.why: The judge said good intentions could not clear him of stealing. He had confessed, so the first option is wrong.

why: 'the court moved to exonerate' is unidiomatic and legally inaccurate; rewritten as the charge being dropped and Rafael exonerated.

set.text: When the dam above the fictional town of Corrin failed one spring, the water reached the streets in less than an hour. For the families who lived there, it was a cataclysm. Hundreds of homes were swept away, and thousands of people were uprooted in a single afternoon, forced to start over somewhere else with only the clothes they wore. Two older residents lost their lives, and the mayor's first public words were a message of condolence to their families. In the weeks that followed, the streets were filled with detritus: broken furniture, tangled fencing, soaked mattresses and children's toys. Yet the response was an outpouring of help from across the country. Trucks arrived with blankets and food, and strangers offered spare rooms. One woman, bereft of her home and her family's photographs, told a reporter that the kindness of strangers was the only thing keeping her going.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “uprooted” mean?
options: moved to a hotel for a holiday
asked to help clean up the streets
forced to leave their homes and settle somewhere new
pulled out of the ground like trees
qs.why: The families lost their homes and had to start over elsewhere, in spare rooms offered by strangers. 'Pulled out of the ground' is the word's literal sense for plants, not people.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “detritus” mean?
options: broken pieces and rubbish left behind
qs.why: The list that follows, broken furniture and soaked mattresses, is waste left by the flood.

qs.q: According to the passage, what helped the woman who lost her home keep going?
options: A new house from the mayor.
Help from her old neighbors in town.
qs.why: She told a reporter that the kindness of strangers was the only thing keeping her going.

why: 'dispossessed' (card: having your land or home taken away from you) implies someone taking it; a flood does not dispossess people. Swapped for the unused level word 'uproot' and rewrote the word question.

set.text: Ten years ago, the drive from the town of Bayview to the city took twenty minutes. Today, at rush hour, Route 9 often sits in gridlock, with cars not moving at all for minutes at a time, and commuters can spend an hour covering eight miles. The reasons are not mysterious. As new housing developments began to proliferate along the highway, the town approved each one separately, without asking where all the new cars would go. Meanwhile, the bus service was allowed to dwindle; there used to be twelve routes, and there are three today. Town engineer Farida Haddad calls the old approach myopic. 'We thought about the tax money each project would bring this year,' she said, 'not about the next twenty.' Her models show that, if nothing changes, travel times will keep rising inexorably as more families move in. Air quality near the highway, she added, is already alarmingly poor on summer afternoons.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “proliferate” mean?
qs.why: More and more developments appeared along the highway.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “myopic” mean?
options: unable to see far with the eyes
focused only on the present, not the future
qs.why: She says they thought about this year, not the next twenty. 'Unable to see far' is the word's literal eye meaning, not the one used here.

qs.q: According to Farida Haddad, what was the town's main mistake?
options: Judging projects by short-term money instead of long-term effects.
Moving the bus station to the city.
qs.why: She says they thought about this year's tax money, not the next twenty years.

why: 'frozen in gridlock' (card: traffic cannot move at all) contradicted the next clause, where cars cover eight miles; now the standstill comes in stretches.
